narration_line: Four years ago I told my mother I wasn't scared. It was the first lie I told at college.
The gate looked bigger than the brochure, my hostel room smaller. I kept the yellow backpack on, just in case.
Meera, my roommate, already knew half the batch. I knew nobody, and smiled like I didn't mind.
Textbooks, a plastic ID card, and lunch in the canteen, where everyone seemed to belong except me.
Then the rain came, and Meera dragged me out of the hostel under her umbrella. Somehow, I laughed.
A boy in a black cap saved me a seat. That was Kabir. By mid-August, I had two friends.
September taught me two things: Kabir's handwriting is a gift, and the library closes at ten sharp.
Samosas became our ritual. Evenings meant the terrace, an orange sky, and home feeling far but bearable.
Every Sunday Maa called, and every Sunday I said I was fine. Then Diwali arrived and every window glowed.
Winter crept in. Papers, panic and pinned-up lists; we all pretended not to look.
January's sky was full of kites, and mine kept tangling. Meera laughed so hard she let go of hers.
Then a senior named Tanvi asked me one question I couldn't answer: why are you here?
Second year began, and suddenly I was the senior pointing others the right way, still without an answer.
I looked for answers in the lab, among wires, blinking lights, and Dev, who talked to circuits like old friends.
November arrived loud, bright and sleepless. The whole college forgot about answers, and so did I.
Ice cream, dancing, and a shelf of tiny trophies none of us won. Best fest of my life.
Sunday arrived quietly. For a few hours, I forgot my question.
Winter again: borrowed scarves, steaming mugs, and nights that refused to end.
Summer break: four of us, one overnight bus, and Manali somewhere at the end of a very bendy road.
Nobody spoke for a while. For once, nobody needed to.
Cold fingers, a wobbly bridge, and bravery borrowed from Meera. I did not tell Maa about the bridge.
The market sold woollen caps. Kabir bought two, then met snow and lost the argument immediately.
Smoke in our clothes, a guitar nobody could play, and four exhausted heads on the long ride back.
Third year handed us one big idea and no idea how to build it. Dev said: we'll figure it out.
Months of tangled wires and failed tests. We were so sure we were close.
The review panel said our idea would never work. Afterwards Tanvi asked again: why are you here?
I didn't sleep. I went to the lake at sunrise and decided to try again, scared, but trying.
One winter weekend, we rebuilt everything on cans and stubbornness. And then, impossibly, the judges clapped.
Afterwards came quiet afternoons at the cafe, flat whites, and a road covered in red petals. I almost felt brave.
That summer, an internship: a lanyard, a desk of my own, and the odd feeling of being taken seriously.
Final year began with sunset walks, one printed resume, and a lot of quiet worry about what came next.
Then placement season: a borrowed blazer, polished shoes, and a corridor full of people pretending not to be nervous.
Five days of waiting. I checked my phone forty times before lunch. Then, one message.
I read it four times. Then I ran, and Meera was already running too. The whole city glowed.
Home for winter. Over tea, Maa asked how I really was. For the first time, I didn't say fine.
Final semester. January mist, one last demo day, and a camera I kept raising before the moments could slip away.
Holi turned the courtyard into a paint box, and nobody stayed clean.
Then the goodbyes began quietly: returned library books, an empty classroom, a bare mattress. Everything echoed.
Handwritten cards, one last sunset on the auditorium steps, and string lights over everyone I'd miss.
Five cups, clinked. Black gowns, thrown caps. Tanvi once asked why I came. Now I knew: to find these four.
I walked out through the same gate, scared again, the yellow backpack still on my shoulder.
I called Maa from the window seat and told the truth. She laughed. She'd known since the first Sunday.
